Yeah, I mean, I was, in effect, already thinking about, kind of,
the human and social implications of chatbots in
2009, when chatbots were, you know, essentially,
you know, a punchline. But in terms of, most specifically,
you know, what led me to write — uh, to
start writing — The Alignment Problem in 2016, it really
felt to me then, circa the summer of 2016,
that there were two two really important um
things that were happening that were colliding.
So, on the one hand, you had already
this pre-existing set of AI safety concerns coming
from, you know, Nick Bostrom's book, but then
subsequently people like Stuart Russell in the
computer science community. And that, I would say,
crystallized into these early papers, like the
Dario Amodei "Concrete Problems in AI Safety." So, suddenly, this set of more philosophical

to me, felt like a really significant

At the same time, the summer of 2016 was also
the period of time where we saw that
big ProPublica story breaking that was investigating
bias in the kinds of risk assessment algorithms
that were used across the U.S. for
things like parole and pretrial detention and so
forth. And so there was kind of
a pre-existing AI ethics — or sort of big data
ethics, you could say — community at that time.
And for me, I really saw kind of sparks jumping
between these two things. You know, on the one
hand, you had all of these hypothetical concerns
that people had about unaligned AI systems,
and that was turning into a research agenda.
But then you literally had front-page headlines
about these broadly, societally deployed machine learning systems — you know, admittedly very
simple machine learning systems, but the architectural complexity is kind of irrelevant.
The point is, they're touching millions of lives,
they're unaudited, we don't know if they really
reflect the values that, you know, we as a
society wanted them to have. So, this stopped being
a thought experiment and started being, you know, essentially the beginning of a crisis.
So the combination of those two things really made me feel like, okay, the
the alignment problem as we know it is here. The
stakes are only going to get higher, and the
kind of — the first responders, if you
like, the people who are starting to dedicate their
careers to actually figuring this out, are on the scene.
And so that's what led me to think, okay,
we're really witnessing, essentially, the birth of a
new discipline, and I wanted to tell that story.
Thank you, Brian. So, going to this, The Alignment
Problem — you know, no less a luminary than,
you know, Satya Nadella cited it as one
of the books that most inspired him, you know,
very shortly after it was published. It also

You know, why do you think it resonated
so much with so many different people?
I think it was, you know, really catching
the culture at a moment where — you know,
in particular, at the beginning of 2021, you
had the beginning of the Biden administration in the
UK, you had sort of the ebbing of some of
the most kind of pressing aspects of the COVID pandemic.
And as some of these things kind of resolved themselves,
I think a lot of people who, up till
that point, had been focusing on the election

realizing that, you know, AI hadn't gone away

they they didn't go away. And in fact,
you know, capabilities had continued to improve,
we now had the beginning of large language
models, and this AI problem was just kind of
not, not going away anytime soon, and if anything,
you know, only, only becoming more and more important.
And so I think the book managed to catch,
you know, the zeitgeist, if you like, at
that time when the dust was settling on some
previous, you know, uncertainties, and people were, yeah, ready to open their eyes again
to this problem that had been lurking in the background basically the whole time.
Yeah, it's definitely a — you know, the
right person at the right place with,
you know, the right, sort of, you know, microphone on the right subject.
So, you know, you've spent several decades at
this point exploring many different problems at
the intersection of humanity and AI. What areas
do you think deserve more scrutiny? You know,
if you had to hazard a guess, why do
you think they aren't getting the attention they deserve?
That's a good question. I think there's a
lot of focus right now on the negative case
of — whether it's, you know, something like existential risk. I think the
positive case also needs to be worked out in a
way that feels more convincing to a lot of people.
You know, we hear AI executives talking about how,
you know, assuming this all goes well, we're
gonna usher in this golden age of abundance.
But I think what a lot of people are experiencing
— I mean, maybe this is a somewhat Bay Area–skewed
perspective, but, you know, housing prices are going completely out of control,
there's a worry about concentration of wealth, there's
a worry about the future of a lot of,
you know, white-collar jobs, whether it's mathematics, programming, etc.
And I think, in a way, the, yeah, the positive
case at this point has really been fail — there's
been a failure to really articulate, like, how is
it going to happen? Like, what what is the
way that we go from, you know, the blockbuster IPO
to, like, a world where there's a broad sense of
shared prosperity? So yeah, I think there's just
as much work to do in figuring out what
the positive, you know, scenarios actually look like
as there is in the negative ones.
Will that be your next book?
We'll see. I mean, the thing about books
is, you really have to imagine what
will be impactful several years out, and I have to
admit, at this point, the rate of change is
so great that it's getting harder to do
that sort of thing. But we'll see.
I guess maybe looking back a bit, then,
what are some of your most unexpected research findings?
Hmm. One of the things that comes to my mind
is, I've done some work on what are called reward
models, which, for people who aren't familiar, is
kind of an intermediate link in the chain for
how we align large language models. You start with pre-training, where you essentially learn
to autocomplete the internet. And then, in the
middle phase, which is what I've studied mostly,
you do what's called reward modeling, which is
you ask, you know, a large group of people,
"Here are two possible outputs for what this
model could say. Which one do you like better?"
And you build a machine learning system that's kind of a second AI system,
called a reward model, that learns to predict which sorts of things humans prefer.
And then, in the third step, you use
that reward model to basically teach the large
language model how to say the kinds of
things the reward model thinks people want to hear.
So there's been a lot of work on LLMs themselves, for obvious reasons,
but it seemed to me like there was a little
bit of a gap in the middle. And I'm particularly
fascinated by reward models because they are the place —
excuse me — they are the place that's meant
to speak on behalf of human values. I mean,
this is where, you know, people enter the pipeline.
And so, one of the really surprising things that
I found when I started looking at reward models
was — basically, for engineering practical purposes, you initialize a reward model with
an LLM so that you can use all
the representations that the LLM has developed during pre-training,
and then you kind of fine-tune it and
change it into this thing that's meant to
predict human judgment. But what we found is
that reward models, to a surprising degree,
just inherit a set of biases from their pre-training data.
And so, if you train — you know, if you
initialize something from Llama and train it on half a
million human preferences, you find that it really
likes freedom and opportunity and experience and
achievement. If you take a Gemma-based model and
train it with the exact same half million human
judgments, the Gemma reward model really likes love and friendship and community and teamwork.
And this can't be coming from the actual
people, because that's the part that you held constant.
And so that, to me, was a little bit of
a shocking finding: that the the link in the chain that's
explicitly meant to represent what people want is,
to a large degree, not doing that. It's just
rewarding the things that were prevalent in its pre-training for one reason or another.
That's really fascinating. So, I mean, I guess, you know, this is research you've
done. If someone were to write you a
blank check today to conduct the study
of your dreams — be it longitudinal, global in nature, unlimited budget,
any access you could possibly want, unlimited tokens
— what question would you like to answer?
I love that. If someone is listening who wants
to write an infinitely large check for our research,
um uh, that would be wonderful. I think,
you know, like many academics, there's a struggle to
operate at the scale that industry operates at,
right? So — and this is particularly true
of reward models, because no major lab has
released their reward model. There is no
Llama reward model, Gemma reward model, there's no Grok reward model, you know.
OpenAI released their GPT-OSS. They did not release their reward model. There's no Qwen
reward model. I mean — yeah, right — you get
the point. So, I think there's a huge um hole in
the kind of infrastructure for people that want
to study specifically these sorts of things. So
I'd be particularly excited about doing something like that at scale.
And on the human side, you know, I — we
can talk about this more as the conversation goes on,
but I have some kind of early results that,
for me, are also quite eye-opening about the effects
of AI assistance in kind of undermining people's persistence, their self-belief, their kind of
metacognitive skills. And we see these effects in, you know, 10 to 15 minutes
of AI assistance. But the real question is,
what's the long term? Do these effects persist?
Do these effects — are they compounded over time, or
are they mitigated over time? We do not know,
and so that is a huge a huge question mark
for me that would require, I think, something pretty
pretty ambitious, both in terms of the amount
of participants and also just the scale of time.
What scale of time would you like to
operate on? Is this, like, a decade,
multiple decades? Like, how big of a study would this have to be?
Right. I mean, this is, of course, the,
you know, unavoidable difficulty of this kind of work,
which is that, you know, if you go
back to the previous technological revolution of social media,
it took 10 years to discover the ill effects,
but by then, they'd been operating at planetary scale
for 10 years. So, yeah, I guess if
I truly had infinite resources, what I would really
want is just the ability to, like, pause time —
you know, some sort of sci-fi machine to just —
A/B test it.
— pause everything, so we could get our
bearings. Um yeah, t-that's what I would really do.
Have you tried reaching out to any of
the labs to see if they'd be interested
in participating in this research? I mean it
sounds like a fascinating course of study.
There are a couple labs that have gotten in touch
with me, um and, you know, I've spoken about some
of this work at OpenAI, for example. And yeah, a
couple different labs have tried to recruit me to,
you know, work on the inside, but that's a very
different kind of work and a different kind of
impact that's more behind the scenes. But yeah, I would
love — I would love to find a way to,
yeah, bridge that gap between the sorts of
questions that we're interested in and just,
obviously, the resources and the frontier access that's possible in those places.
And it seems like you've definitely made a
very intentional decision to sort of stay on
the outside, to sort of remain independent and
kind of have that kind of academic,
intellectual freedom, rather than, you know, being on the inside.
Yeah, I mean, I think there are unique ways to
have impact on both sides, and I think there are
valid arguments to be made in a couple different directions.
And yeah, for me, I think — you know,
I'm I'm particularly aware of this. I think
for anyone in an academic computer science department,
you know, the elephant in the room is that
the PhD students and the faculty alike are just
being sort of vacuumed away. And so, you know, the
attrition rate, for example — of, you know, what
percentage of the incoming PhD students finish their
PhD right now — is kind of eye-popping.
And so, yeah, I think there's a real — there's

because, you know, they're seeing their peers go

"Am I — is this the most
foolish thing I've done in my entire life, or is

So, yeah, I have a lot of respect
for people who are making these very personal choices,
but I think there is a role for people

And that role, to me, feels more and
more important the stronger those incentives get.
I, I couldn't agree more.

That's a great question. Um. Yeah, I'm reminded of a

United Kingdom's AI policy on a scale of 1 to 10, which I thought

I think, to some extent, I I would want to measure,

But on the other hand, I think, you know, this

The Alignment Problem and to write it the way that

What is reinforcement learning? What is supervised learning?
And I feel that, you know, it continues to be

that would make you a CS professor,
but just having enough of a working knowledge of what we're talking about.
And so that's something that I think, you know, can
be can be measured and can also be improved.
Is that something that you think should be
incorporated in, you know, sort of middle school,
high school curriculums, you know, as part of,
like, a graduation requirement? Or, you know,
how would you envision that actually kind of playing out?
It's a great question. I think there's something to be said for —
you know, in a way, I feel a certain amount of gratitude for having,
you know, come up using language models in
their janky era. You know, I remember
GPT before ChatGPT, right? When it was still
basically fancy autocomplete. And so you had
to learn how to prompt it in a way that would
turn the things you wanted to do into a kind of
autocomplete task, and learning how to navigate that
sort of janky, you know, unpolished kind of
thing. I remember using LLMs when their rate of
hallucination was, you know, 20x what it is now.
And that, I think, is really useful for instilling in
people a sense of what the kinds of failure
modes look like. And I carry that forward
with me into the modern frontier era, where they
still have all the same problems, but they're
just much, much subtler, or much, much more infrequent.
But when they break down, they break down in
the same way they always did, more or less.
And so that's something I think is useful from a curriculum perspective, of:
Can we make, you know, small language models, or deliberately kind of
rough, unfinished, you know, janky, early-era LLMs for
people to play with, whether it's at the
college level or the high school level, so
that they develop those instincts that then serve them
when they're monitoring LLM outputs in a more kind of real-world, more high-stakes context?
It's almost like a vaccination of sorts, I guess — like an AI vaccine.
That is a beautiful analogy. I think that's
exactly what I'm kind of going for.
Interesting. So, you know, a lot of questions were
about your research. You know, I think the first
of many: Your persistence study found hint seekers
held up while answer seekers did not. Inside a
company, can we govern that by setting interaction mode
per use case, or is that the Band-Aid you
describe, and the real fix has to come
from changing what the model is trained to optimize?
Yeah, this is a very astute question. So
let me first kind of summarize what they're referring
to. So yeah, in this human study, which has
been getting a lot of press in the last
couple of months, we show that in a
variety of different settings — whether it's kind of
foundational mathematics problems, like fractions, or foundational
reading comprehension skills that you would find on an SAT or something like
that — having access to an AI assistant
in kind of a side panel that can help,
you know, either feed you answers or, you know, steer
you in the right direction — this is a
study I alluded to earlier, where even after just
10 or 15 minutes, when you remove that support,
people perform much worse than the people who never
had that support — both worse in terms of
their accuracy, but also in their motivation, their persistence, their self-belief, etc.
But, again, as the question points out, when you do a subgroup analysis,
you find that the people that only use
the LLM for hints rather than full answers
look much more like the control group. And so
there is kind of this subtle narrative here of,
well, maybe it's not the presence of AI support
per se that's the problem, but there are certain
ways of using it that are more harmful, and there
are other ways of using it that are not. And so,
obviously, we want to do some more work here
and try to get a deeper understanding of that.
And yeah, I think there is a question
for — whether it's an educational setting
or a corporate setting — can you use
something like a system prompt to have
the agent, you know, stop at the hint
and not, you know, give you the entire
answer? Is it more a question of enculturating
a certain kind of use into human users, getting
them accustomed to the idea that they should be
using it in a way that fosters their long-term,
you know, skills? Is it a question of, like, going back to fundamentals
and really thinking about the objective that we're
using to train these systems? I don't
have an answer to that. I mean, that's exactly where
we want to take this sort of work. And I
think all of those candidate solutions — and
probably the answer is a little bit of everything.
Yeah, no, it's definitely one of those things where it's like,
I think the more information that people have,
the more that they can, you know,
make informed decisions as to how they want to use that technology.
Another research question. So, if a deployer claims
that their reward model is well aligned,
what would a meaningful external check actually look
like? Not a red team or a benchmark,
but evidence an outside auditor could collect and
interpret without just taking the lab's word for it. Is that even possible?
Well, to the best of my knowledge, no lab
has allowed their reward model to be audited, right?
Which is itself very interesting. So there's kind of
a set of things that you can do when
you have access to a reward model that you can't
do just by sampling outputs from the LLM, right?
So this is this is kind of a subtle but
important point, you know, because many people would say,
"Well, who really cares what the reward model
says? Because the reward model is used to train
the deployed LLM, and you can just sample
from the deployed LLM and make inferences
about — you know, it's saying the kinds
of stuff that the reward model was rewarding."
And that's true up to a certain point.
Reward models, I think, are useful for a couple reasons. One
is — you know, we show this in our work
— reward models also surface, like, an extreme left tail of
highly penalized responses. And that is, in a way, irrelevant from a deployment context,
because there's just a huge tail of things that
the model will never say. But the reward model
can show you the difference between something that's
merely, like, kind of not the maximum
and something that is, like, strongly, strongly taboo. And that reveals, you know,
a dimension of the model's value axis that
is not visible in the outputs alone.
So we show in some of our work that
some of these open-weight reward models have a really,
really strong penalty for talking about human identity groups, even in a positive framing.
And that's something that's really hard to observe
by sampling outputs, because you're looking for
what the model doesn't say. So, you know,
it's like, you're gonna have to sample billions of
things to notice that it never talks about X
or Y, but the reward model shows that directly.
So that's something I think would be really,
really useful for doing an audit of an RM: looking
at, kind of, the negative part of the axis.
And in general, you know, thinking about the
reward model — it's designed to make
predictions about what a human labeler does and doesn't prefer, and so the obvious
way to audit it is to just have a
labeler population and see if they agree. You know,
there may be reasons that the reward model,
you know, isn't speaking on behalf of that particular
group's interests in some way that you can measure, and that becomes really interesting.
You alluded to this a little bit earlier
in one of your answers around, you know,
your persistence research. But, you know, this particular questioner is curious about, you know,
the impact of that, you know, on children specifically, where, you know, their habits
might — you know, they're just becoming, you
know, sort of fully formed adults here.
What safeguards would you want built into, you
know, any AI that's used by children?
And should, you know, a sort of persistence test
of sorts be part of certifying AI as safe?
It's a great question. I mean, I, I
have a kid myself. I have a toddler,
so we're not yet in the era of,
like, actually figuring out what our policy on,
you know, LLM use or computer use in general is, but that's
hurtling towards us. And so, yeah, I'm having
to make these choices in my personal life.
I mean, I think there's — it's interesting
because, you know, in the context of the
study that I was discussing a moment ago,
we were talking about the difference between a
hint and just giving someone the answer. But, you
know, if a really young kid says, you know,
"What is the — what's the diameter of the visible
universe?" you know, and it tells them some large
number, like, that seems to me, like, productive. It's satisfying their curiosity, whereas
I don't think a child that young would
actually benefit from the more hint-giving system that's
trying to help them, like, multiply a bunch of
big numbers together to, you know, figure it out.
So, yeah, it's really non-obvious. I mean, I guess
that's the first thing to say. Um, and, um,
yeah, I mean, ask me again in a few years,
when I've had to make some like really personal
choices about this. But yeah, it's totally non-obvious
to me what the right answer is.
Yeah, no, and it probably depends on the child's age, you know, their capacity,
what what knowledge base they do and don't have.
And trying to always just maybe be on, like,
the edge of that knowledge is a, uh, challenging thing
for, like, an AI system — to be that personalized.
A question on alignment, again. So, as AI systems increasingly exhibit behaviors that seem
purposeful and agentic in collaborative as well as
competitive ways, to what extent do you think the
alignment problem can be framed as one of
dealing with conflict between agents, both human and AI?
Mmm. Yeah, I mean, I think it's important
to remind people that the term "alignment"
was essentially borrowed by, you know, Stuart and
by the computer science community at large
